title: CRA Reporting Desk: Cyber Resilience Act reporting and SBOM for small product makers
source: Top 25 SaaS ideas for Victor (research report, Nov 2026)
summary: Helps small device and software makers meet the EU Cyber Resilience Act's 24-hour vulnerability-reporting clock, with ready report drafts and an up-to-date list of the software parts in each product (SBOM).
hook: "If a vulnerability in our device were exploited tomorrow, I honestly don't know who would file the report, or where."
story:
**Lukas is CTO of a 30-person smart-home device maker in Austria.** Since 11 September 2026, the Cyber Resilience Act says that if a vulnerability in one of his products is actively exploited, he must send an **early warning within 24 hours** and a full notification within **72 hours** through ENISA's reporting platform. He has no security response team and no list of all the open-source parts in his firmware.

Enterprise tools like Black Duck are far beyond his budget, and consultants are slow. With CRA Reporting Desk, his team imports an **SBOM for each product**, gets alerts when a component is **actively exploited**, and when it happens a **countdown clock** starts with AI-drafted report text in ENISA's field structure.
whyNow: This is the strongest legal deadline in the report. Since 11 September 2026, every maker of a product with digital elements sold in the EU must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform: a 24-hour early warning, a 72-hour notification, then a final report. Full obligations, including a machine-readable SBOM, follow on 11 December 2027.
evidence: Since 11 September 2026: 24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification and a final report for actively exploited vulnerabilities, via ENISA's Single Reporting Platform [Noerr / usd.de]
CRA fines reach €15M or 2.5% of global turnover (secondary source) [advisori]
Full CRA obligations, including a machine-readable SBOM, apply from 11 December 2027 [SafeDep]
ENISA's 2026 SME survey (194 organisations, 31 countries): 66% had heard of the CRA, but incident-response and lifecycle maturity was only 2.6 out of 5 [ENISA]
73% of surveyed SMEs asked for documentation templates and 71% for secure-development templates [ENISA]

whyReal.title: The deadline is already live
whyReal.text: Reporting duties started on 11 September 2026, and fines reach €15M or 2.5% of global turnover (secondary source).

whyReal.title: SMEs are not ready
whyReal.text: ENISA found incident-response maturity of only 2.6 out of 5, and the survey probably over-represents the more prepared firms.

whyReal.title: They ask for templates
whyReal.text: 73% want documentation templates and 71% secure-development templates: exactly what the product provides.

whyReal.title: No SMB-priced tool found
whyReal.text: Enterprise tools and consultancies exist, but no self-serve CRA workflow tool with public pricing was found. And it is a perfect fit for Victor's security skills.

whoPays.label: Customer
whoPays.text: Small and medium companies (5–250 staff) that sell connected or software products in the EU: IoT and embedded device makers, smart-home and industrial gadget firms, desktop and mobile software vendors, including non-EU makers selling into the EU.

whoPays.label: Buyer
whoPays.text: The CTO, head of engineering or founder. CRA consultants could resell it.

whoPays.label: Start market
whoPays.text: EU product makers plus non-EU makers selling into the EU, in English.

solution.title: SBOM import or generation
solution.text: wrapping the open-source Syft/CycloneDX tools, plus a GitHub Action.

solution.title: Vulnerability matching
solution.text: through OSV, with an "actively exploited" flag from the US CISA KEV list.

solution.title: Intake and disclosure
solution.text: a vulnerability intake form plus a security.txt and disclosure-policy generator.

solution.title: Countdown and drafts
solution.text: a 24h / 72h / final-report clock with AI-drafted text in ENISA's field structure.

solution.title: Audit log and notifications
solution.text: every step logged; customer-notification templates ready.

timeline.what: **Validate, no code.** Publish a landing page ("Meet the CRA's 24-hour reporting deadline without a security team") with a free downloadable "CRA reporting runbook" PDF. Post in embedded/IoT communities and on LinkedIn, and cold-email 100 small IoT makers. Success = 20+ email sign-ups and 5+ booked calls.
Victor builds the inventory, SBOM import/generation and OSV/KEV matching.
Intake form, security.txt generator, countdown clock with AI drafts, audit log.
First paying product makers; approach CRA consultants as resellers.

risks.risk: Technical buyers are hard for Jonatan to sell to
risks.answer: Jonatan books the calls; Victor joins them. Use CRA consultants as resellers.

risks.risk: Legal liability if a draft is wrong
risks.answer: Position it as a workflow tool, not legal advice; a human always submits.

risks.risk: Big security vendors could add the same features
risks.answer: Stay SMB-priced and self-serve; move fast while the deadline is new.

risks.risk: ENISA's form may change; market limited to product makers
risks.answer: Keep field mappings configurable; target the many small IoT and software makers.

questions: If a vulnerability in your product were exploited tomorrow, who would file the CRA report, and how?

What have you spent or budgeted on CRA readiness (consultants, tools, staff time)?
If a tool handled the deadline clock, report drafts and SBOM, what would it need to do for you to pay €100–200 a month?
